name: Widest banner between two posts
brief:
Posts stand one metre apart along a trading-floor wall, and `posts[i]` is the height of post `i` in metres. A banner hangs between two posts `i < j`. Its width is `j - i` and its height is the shorter of the two posts, so its area is `min(posts[i], posts[j]) * (j - i)`.

Write `widest_banner(posts)`, which returns the largest area any banner can have, or 0 when there are fewer than two posts.

Example. For `posts = [2, 5, 1, 4]` the banner between the 5 and the 4 is 4 high and 2 wide, area 8. No pair does better, so the answer is 8.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 100{,}000$ posts, each a whole number between $0$ and $10^6$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Trying every pair is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Start with the two end posts. The shorter of the pair caps every narrower banner that uses it, so move that pointer inwards.

examples.note: The 5 and the 4 give 4 times 2. The two ends give only 2 times 3.
Two posts 1 metre apart, both 3 high, give area 3.

tests.call: widest_banner([1000000 - abs(50000 - i) for i in range(100001)])

how: Submit runs 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Every narrower banner that keeps the shorter post is no taller and no wider, so that post can be dropped.
Moving the taller post instead can drop the best pair, as in `[1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]`.
Each step drops one post, so the work is $O(n)$.

planted.slip: Moving the taller post inwards can throw away the post that belongs to the best banner.
Counting posts, `j - i + 1`, instead of the gaps between them makes every banner one metre too wide.
Taking the taller post as the height lets the banner hang above the shorter post.
